name: Posidippus
bio: Posidippus, a Macedonian poet of the third century BC, was one of the leading epigrammatists of the early Hellenistic age. His poems range from love epigrams to epitaphs and dedications.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him without qualification; the uncertain ones are filed as anonymous.

poems.title: Book V, 134
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: Shower on us, O Attic jug, the dewy rain of Bacchus ; shower it and refresh our merry picnic. Let Zeno, the learned swan, be kept silent, and Cleanthes’ Muse, and let our converse be of Love the bitter-sweet.

poems.title: Book V, 183
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: We are four at the party, and each brings his mistress ; since that makes eight, one jar of Chian is not enough. Go, my lad, to Aristius and tell him the first he sent was only half full; it is two gallons short certainly ; I think more. But look sharp, for we all meet at five.

poems.title: Book V, 186
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: Don’t think to deceive me, Philaenis, with your plausible tears. I know; you love absolutely no one more than me, as long as you are lying beside me; but if you were with someone else, you would say you loved him more than me.

poems.title: Book V, 211
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: Tears and revel, why do you incite me before my feet are out of the flame to rush into another of Cypris’ fires? Never do I cease from love, and tireless desire ever brings me some new pain from Aphrodite.

poems.title: Book V, 213
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: It anyone is with Pythias, I am off, but if she sleeps alone, for God’s sake admit me for a little, and say for a token that drunk, and through thieves, I came with daring Love for my guide.

poems.title: Book VII, 170
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.note: Attribution doubtful in Paton (Posidippus or Callimachus).
poems.text: The dumb image of himself attracted Archianax the three year old boy, as he was playing by the well. His mother dragged him all dripping from the water, asking herself if any life was left in him. The child defiled not with death the dwelling of the Nymphs, but fell asleep on his mother’s knees, and slumbers sound.

poems.title: Book VII, 267
poems.author: Posidippus
poems.text: Sailors, why do you bury me near the sea? Far away from it ye should have built the poor tomb of the shipwrecked man. I shudder at the noise of the waves my destroyers. Yet even so I wish you well for taking pity on Nicetas.
